subject: Civil Engineering
title: Transparent and Light-Transmitting Concrete
description: A micro-lesson that makes Transparent and Light-Transmitting Concrete usable.

hook.text: Concrete that lets light through — thousands of optical fibers embedded in a solid wall.

buildup.text: LiTraCon (light-transmitting concrete) was invented in Hungary in 2001 by Áron Losonczi.

discovery.text: Optical fibers run from one face to the other — light passes through, but the wall is solid.

twist.text: Shadows of people on one side are visible as silhouettes on the other — a living wall.

climax.text: The National Theatre of Abu Dhabi uses translucent concrete panels in its facade.

punchline.text: Concrete that glows with daylight — material science at its most poetic.

quiz.question: How does light-transmitting concrete work?
options: The concrete is poured very thin so light passes through directly
Optical fibers embedded through the wall carry light from one face to the other
Phosphorescent chemicals in the mix glow after absorbing sunlight

details.summary: Light-transmitting concrete, or translucent concrete, embeds optical fibers or transparent polymers in standard concrete to transmit light through wall panels while maintaining structural integrity. Shadows of objects on one side appear on the opposite side, creating dramatic architectural effects.
details.whyItMatters: Translucent concrete combines the strength and fire resistance of concrete with natural light transmission, offering new architectural possibilities for facades, partitions, and decorative elements.
takeaways: Optical fibers transmit light through concrete panels up to 200 mm thick
Structural properties remain comparable to standard concrete
Applications include facades, interior partitions, and illuminated surfaces

faq.question: How does light pass through solid concrete?
faq.answer: Thousands of optical fibers running perpendicular to the panel surface carry light from one face to the other by total internal reflection. The concrete matrix between fibers remains completely opaque.

faq.question: Is light-transmitting concrete used in real buildings?
faq.answer: Yes. Notable examples include the Italian Pavilion at the 2010 Shanghai Expo, decorative wall panels in European buildings, and underground parking structures where it transmits natural light.
